criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to piped drinking-water supply and supply intermittency across central and peripheral municipalities of the Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region (RMRJ).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading diverge (passes plain wording; fails narrow rule-type reading). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study passes because it discusses metropolitan institutional and governance arrangements, including municipal delegation of WSS services to state-owned utility CEDAE, the 1974 statutory merger creating RMRJ and CEDAE (Lei Complementar No. 20), a bulk-water supply contract with private concessionaire Aguas de Niteroi, and centralized top-down planning versus inter-municipal cooperation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, however, it fails: as the authors explicitly note, their empirical analysis focuses on the socio-technical characteristics and path-dependence of centralized physical trunk infrastructure (dependence on single bulk sources, insufficient adduction flow, absence of local distribution reservoirs causing low pipe pressure, and core-biased historical capital projects like Guandu II), while political and institutional history serves as macro-governance background rather than an empirical evaluation of a rule-type mechanism (such as tenure or documentation rules, eligibility screening, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or ownership/regulatory rules directly governing household access).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical evidence from a three-year diachronic descriptive case study combining semi-structured/key-informant interviews (CEDAE commercial and metropolitan distribution directors, local DAE operational technicians, and river basin officials), planning documents, utility hydraulic flow data, and 1980 and 2010 IBGE census statistics.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports municipal-level percentages of households connected to the public water supply network versus wells/springs or rainwater harvesting (Tables 3, 6, and 7) as well as qualitative field and interview evidence on intermittent supply (e.g., water delivered only two to three days per week and multi-month outages in Baixada Fluminense).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (water supply systems and constituent municipalities/households of West and East RMRJ), the socio-technical infrastructure exposure, the household coverage and continuity outcomes, and the diachronic descriptive case-study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (eligible without translation).

study_design: Diachronic descriptive single-case study (three years of qualitative fieldwork with key-informant interviews, historical/policy document analysis, and descriptive secondary census and hydraulic data)
population_and_sample: Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region (RMRJ; 11,835,708 inhabitants across 21 municipalities, focusing on 13 municipalities in West and East RMRJ served by the Guandu-Lages-Acari and Imunana-Laranjal systems), supplemented by key-informant interviews with CEDAE directors, local DAE technicians, and river basin staff
exposure: Socio-technical path-dependence of centralized macro-scale water supply infrastructure (single-source trunk networks, insufficient adduction capacity, lack of local storage reservoirs, and historical core-favoring capital investment overseen by state utility CEDAE)
outcome: Municipal-level household access to the public piped water supply network (%) and reliance on wells/springs or rainwater harvesting (1980 and 2010 IBGE census), plus qualitative evidence of supply intermittency and multi-month service interruptions
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. The paper empirically examines household water network coverage and supply intermittency across RMRJ municipalities using IBGE census data, technical records, and three years of fieldwork interviews (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it discusses metropolitan institutional governance, municipal delegation to state utility CEDAE, historical state reorganization, and bulk-supply contracting. Under the active rule-type scope, however, its empirical explanatory focus is the physical/socio-technical path-dependence of centralized macro-infrastructure (trunk pipeline capacities, missing storage reservoirs, and core-biased capital engineering plans) with institutional history serving only as macro-governance background rather than analyzing a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule governing household access.
